meta.title: Who really said "That Is Part of the Beauty of All Literature. You Discover that Your Longings Are Universal Longings"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not from a Fitzgerald book. The line is Sheilah Graham's recollection of what he told her, published in her 1958 memoir Beloved Infidel.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'That Is Part of the Beauty of All Literature. You Discover that Your Longings Are Universal Longings'?
meta.ogDescription: Fitzgerald said it, according to one witness: Sheilah Graham, who printed it in her 1958 memoir Beloved Infidel, about two decades later.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Fitzgerald, and the credit does trace to one specific book — but not to one of his. The line is a remark Sheilah Graham says he made to her in Hollywood, first printed in her 1958 memoir Beloved Infidel about two decades after the conversation; it has not been found in anything he wrote — Quote Investigator traces it only to Graham’s memoir, and Wikiquote’s Fitzgerald page does not carry it at all.

source.excerpt: “Sheilo,” said Scott. “That is part of the beauty of all literature. You discover that your longings are universal longings, that you’re not lonely and isolated from anyone. You belong.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traced the line to Sheilah Graham and Gerold Frank’s memoir Beloved Infidel: The Education of a Woman (Henry Holt and Company, New York, 1958), chapter 22, page 260 — a citation QI marks ‘Verified on paper’ against the first edition.

The 1958 Henry Holt edition is scanned at the Internet Archive ↗, whose catalogue record confirms the publisher and the year. The scan is lending-restricted, so the page has to be borrowed rather than searched.

WIST Quotations ↗ files it the same way — a comment to Sheilah Graham, c. 1938, quoted in Beloved Infidel, chapter 22 — and cites Quote Investigator as its source, so it corroborates the filing rather than the finding.
Wikiquote’s F. Scott Fitzgerald page ↗ does not carry the line at all, in any of its sections — a useful reminder that its fame has outrun its paper trail.
source.excerptNote: Graham’s transcription of the moment, as reproduced by Quote Investigator from page 260 of the 1958 first edition. Fitzgerald had been reading her Keats’s ‘Ode on a Grecian Urn’ and Marvell’s ‘To His Coy Mistress’; she was struck that love written down centuries ago looked like her own, and this was his reply.

source.rightsNote: Not public domain. The words are Fitzgerald’s as reported, but the only text that originally documents them is Graham and Frank’s Beloved Infidel, first published by Henry Holt in 1958 — long after the 1931 cut-off, so it is treated here as in copyright. Fitzgerald’s own books published before 1931, including The Great Gatsby (1925), are public domain in the United States; this sentence is not in any of them.

author.name: F. Scott Fitzgerald
author.heading: About F. Scott Fitzgerald
author.bio: Francis Scott Fitzgerald was born in Saint Paul, Minnesota on 24 September 1896 and died in Los Angeles on 21 December 1940, aged 44. He is best known for The Great Gatsby (1925), alongside This Side of Paradise (1920) and Tender Is the Night (1934). He spent his last years in Hollywood writing for the studios, where the columnist Sheilah Graham became his companion — and the only witness to this remark.

copyAttribution: "That is part of the beauty of all literature. You discover that your longings are universal longings, that you're not lonely and isolated from anyone. You belong." — F. Scott Fitzgerald, as recalled by Sheilah Graham in Beloved Infidel: The Education of a Woman (New York: Henry Holt and Company, 1958), 260. Attributed: the wording rests on Graham's memoir, published about two decades after the conversation, not on anything Fitzgerald wrote. Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: What gets it wrong
misattribution.intro: Nobody pins this line on the wrong person. The problem is that almost nobody pins it to the right book — it circulates as though Fitzgerald wrote it, when it survives only because a Hollywood columnist wrote down what he said.

items.why: The line is posted almost everywhere as a bare Fitzgerald quotation with no book attached: the Goodreads entry ↗ carries it with 6,597 likes and no source citation at all. Quote Investigator ↗ found its origin in Graham’s memoir rather than anywhere in Fitzgerald’s writings.

A subtitle file for the film adaptation opens the speech ‘The beauty of literature is that it’s ageless’ instead of ‘That is part of the beauty of all literature’. Quote Investigator ↗ logs the variant but states it has not verified that line against the film’s audio track, so the screen wording should be treated as unconfirmed rather than as a second attestation.

F. Scott Fitzgerald on Writing, the anthology edited by Larry W. Phillips and first published in 1986 (Open Library ↗), reprints the remark and cites Beloved Infidel, page 196. Quote Investigator’s inspection of the 1958 first edition puts it at page 260 and notes that page numbers vary between editions — so a bare page reference for this line tells you very little on its own.

misattribution.truthLine: The truth is narrower and more human than the poster version. Sometime around 1938, after Fitzgerald had read her Keats and Marvell, he said this to Sheilah Graham — and we have it only because she remembered it and published it in 1958, about two decades later, as Quote Investigator documents ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Graham had built a Hollywood career on an invented biography. In truth she had spent part of her childhood in an orphanage and her formal schooling had stopped at the eighth grade, and she was embarrassed by what she called the ‘tremendous gaps’ in what she knew. When she admitted this to Fitzgerald he did not flinch: he drew up careful book lists and daily reading schedules, wrote long notes in the margins of the texts he handed her, and quizzed her on them, as Quote Investigator ↗ recounts from the memoir.

This remark belongs to that private tutorial. He had been reading her Keats’s ‘Ode on a Grecian Urn’ and Marvell’s ‘To His Coy Mistress’, and she was struck that people centuries dead had wanted what she wanted. The curriculum outgrew them both: Graham eventually wrote an entire book about it, College of One ↗ (1967), subtitled the story of how F. Scott Fitzgerald educated the woman he loved.
detailsBody: Everything about this quotation rests on a single person’s memory. Graham was there; nobody else was. She published the exchange in 1958, about two decades after it happened, and Quote Investigator’s conclusion says so plainly — the accuracy of the statement hinges on her recall.

That is not a reason to throw it out. Graham was a professional writer working with the biographer Gerold Frank, the reading course she describes is well documented, including in her own later book about it, and no one has produced a competing origin for the sentence. It is a reason to label it honestly: a documented report of something Fitzgerald said, not a line lifted from anything he wrote.
context.pull: The line survives because a gossip columnist remembered it — not because Fitzgerald ever wrote it down.

sourcesVerified.claim: The quotation originates in Sheilah Graham and Gerold Frank's memoir Beloved Infidel: The Education of a Woman (Henry Holt and Company, New York, 1958), first edition, chapter 22, page 260, marked 'Verified on paper'; Fitzgerald spoke it to Graham after sharing Keats's 'Ode on a Grecian Urn' and Marvell's 'To His Coy Mistress'; QI concludes the accuracy hinges on Graham's memory. QI also logs a 1959 film subtitle variant it has NOT verified against the audio track, and the 1986 Larry W. Phillips anthology's citation of page 196.

The quote is filed as a comment to Sheilah Graham, c. 1938, quoted in her book Beloved Infidel: The Education of a Woman, chapter 22 (1958), with the 1959 film variant 'The beauty of literature is that it's ageless' noted separately.

The Internet Archive holds a scan of 'Beloved infidel: the education of a woman' by Sheilah Graham, published by Holt, New York, 1958, with Gerold Frank as an associated name; the item is access-restricted and available only through lending.

Wikiquote's F. Scott Fitzgerald page does not contain 'That is part of the beauty of all literature' or 'your longings are universal longings' in any section (Quoted, the per-book sections, Letters, Notebooks, Quotes about, External links).

Sheilah Graham (1904–1988) was a British-born Hollywood gossip columnist; her relationship with F. Scott Fitzgerald ran from July 1937 to 1940; her memoir Beloved Infidel was published in 1958 with co-author Gerold Frank and filmed in 1959 with Gregory Peck and Deborah Kerr; her 1967 book College of One is subtitled the story of how F. Scott Fitzgerald educated the woman he loved.

F. Scott Fitzgerald was born 24 September 1896 in Saint Paul, Minnesota and died 21 December 1940 in Los Angeles, aged 44; he wrote This Side of Paradise (1920), The Great Gatsby (1925) and Tender Is the Night (1934); he returned to Hollywood in the late 1930s, where the columnist Sheilah Graham was his final companion.
'F. Scott Fitzgerald on Writing', compiled/edited by Larry W. Phillips, was first published in 1986 by Scribner.
The Goodreads quote page presents 'That is part of the beauty of all literature...' attributed to F. Scott Fitzgerald with no book or source citation, and shows 6,597 likes.

Beloved Infidel is a memoir by Sheilah Graham and Gerold Frank published by Holt in New York, adapted into a 1959 20th Century Fox film directed by Henry King starring Gregory Peck and Deborah Kerr; the film omits details of Graham's background present in the memoir.
